When the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland) first took control of the department certain abuses were pointed out to him, and he assured us that he would in no instance undertake any work without securing an estimate of the total cost. But we have had evidence time and again that he has not carried out that programme. The minister shakes his head, but I can tell him that in the case of the Guelph post office, the estimate was exceeded by several thousand dollars, and in Alexandria the minister paid $3,500 for a lot that was dear at $1,500, and we do not know what the cost of the Alexandria building is going to be. We would be negligent in our duty if we did not press for information session after session about buildings, the construction of which has been commenced. I have no doubt that the London armoury is like the rest, and that it will cost more than the original estimate.

speechtext: I think the Printing Bureau complain that the Auditor General was slow in sending in his matter, and that after they had printed it, he was very slow in revising the proofs. I believe they disclaim the responsibility for the delay in the issue of that report. That was stated officially by the department. As to the improvements that may be necessary for carrying on the work of the Bureau, I have no doubt that what my hon. friend says is true. There has been a very large increase in the amount of work done. That applies to all the departments. From almost every section of the country applications have come to the Public Works Department either for new works or for enlargements. If the Printing Bureau is in so congested a state as niy hon. friend says it is, of course the matter will have to be taken into consideration. In any case, it would not be provided for in the main estimates, but in the new estimates for 1904-5.

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I think the trouble Is not so- much with the Auditor General as it is with the different departments in not furnishing the material early enough. There is another difficulty. I did my best last year to induce the Minister of Finance to allow the Auditor General to send out his report for each department as soon as it could be got ready. Why should not that be done instead of keeping everything back till the whole publication can be issued ? It would be a great advantage to the members to receive at their homes such portions of the Auditor General's Report as could be got ready before the meeting of parliament, so that they could make themselves familiar with the business which they would have to take up when the House met. Would not the Minister of Public Works lend us his assistance to have this done ?

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I think that is a matter for parliament to deal with.

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: It seems to me it is a matter for the government to deal with.

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I will bring the; matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I would like to Lave the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on this question, as he is an old parliamentarian.

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I do not think any charge of dilatoriness can be laid at the door of the officials of the Printing Bureau. The cause of delay can be ascertained by inquiry as to the date when the last revised proof was received at the Printing Bureau. I agree with my hon. friend, however, that the officials have riot room to do their work as expeditiously as it might be done. With regard to the delay in the issue of last session's ' Hansard,' I think the Debates Committee are now considering a proposition which will probably expedite the composition of the index. As the hon. member for Lennox says, the Printing Bureau performs an important work, and it ought to be provided with the necessary accommodation. When I last visited it, the accommodation in the bindery was nothing short of scandalous. The number of employees was more than double what should be employed in the space provided.

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I would like to say a word about the building in which the Supreme Court sits. I will not raise the question of the fitness of that building for the first court in the land ; but I will draw the attention of the Solicitor General and the government generally to the fact that there is insufficient room either for the library, the clerks or the lawyers. Some time ago we had room to work in the library ; but gradually we have been pushed out of there. At present there are only two tables at which lawyers can work, and I suppose that next year one of these will have to be moved to make room for more books. There used to be a waiting room, but that is now full of books, and it is difficult to turn around in it to get at the books. The lawyers formerly had a robing room, but that is now occupied by one of the clerks of the court. It is all very well to spend $60,000 on steel drawers and rollers, or $6,000 for an elevator to enable our hon. friends to go to their offices easily and comfortably, or $10,000 for new coal sheds ; but some due regard, I should think, ought to be paid to the needs of the first court in Canada. The judges, lawyers and litigants who go there should not be put to all the inconveniences to which they are now subject. This is a question which has occupied the attention of the Public Wprks Department for some time, but' for one reason or another the department seems unable to come to any decision about it. My hon. and learned friend the Solicitor General knows that it is an injustice, not only to the bar but the public generally, that such a state of things should continue.

My hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgraiii) brought to the attention of the minister the question of repairing or rebuilding or enlarging the Supreme Court. I think it is the duty of the government immediately to take this matter in hand. If the Minister of Public Works is not ready to investigate it himself, seeing that this is a government doing its work by commissions, let a commission be appointed to make a full report on the future wants of the country in reference to public buildings in Ottawa. A proposition is now before the House to acquire a lot at the outskirts of the city to build a geological museum. Why such a building should be placed at the out skirts of the city, I cannot understand. People visiting the capital want to look at the geological museum, and it should be close to the parliament buildings. To-day. nearly half the city of Ottawa is rented by the government for offices. If we look for the militia department, instead of finding it where it ought to be, in the public building ; we find that it has been removed half a mile away to the house of a friend of the government who is paid $12,000 a year as rent. If that amount were capitalized, it would pay for a building almost as good as this one. And, as it is with the Militia Department, so it is in a greater or less degree with almost every other. The government have rented houses all over the city and packed them with civil servants. This kind of thing ought to be stopped, and the Dominion of Canada ought to put up buildings of its own to house its servants. The rentals that are now paid, if capitalized, would provide plenty of accommodation. Take, for instance, the building that was rented for tin-purpose of the census. No less than $6,000 a year is paid for that building. If that amount were capitalized at three per cent It would put up a building three times as large and three times as good as the one now occupied. And the same is more

clearly true of the building Rented for the Militia Department.

speechtext: I think the first thing the government should do would be to reduce the civil service. I am sure tlie chairman will remember when the conduct of the government I supported was challenged because they had too many officials. I venture the assertion that they have got one-third more than we ever had. They have not only filled all the public buildings belonging to the government, but they have rented other buildings throughout the city in order to make places for their political friends. Instead of suggesting another elaborate scheme for spending the people's money to obtain more accommodation for a lot of hangers-on, I would advise you to turn out a lot of these men and women you have now in the public offices and who have nothing to do, and pay a proper salary to those who are left and make them do the work. I was informed by a gentleman in one of the departments that in his office the place was so crowded with officials that he could not do as much work, as he could with a far less number. Now would the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Trade and Commerce tell me that these additional civil servants are necessary because the country is prosperous ? It sounds so silly to hear them say that because the country is prosperous, because the farmers are getting a good price for what they have to sell, because the revenue is increasing, therefore it is necessary to increase the number of officials at Ottawa to the extent they have been increased. I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he sanctions that. I remember when he used to condemn the old government for having too many officials, and I thought at one time that he was honest. Now he sits there complacently and laughs when he has got all his family in the civil service getting good salaries, and while he himself occupies an office that he said was a sinecure. I remember when he was told in my presence that the office was not intended to be permanent, that when the controllers became full fledged ministers tlmt office would be abolished. Yet he was a member of tlie government who, when they made tlie controllers full fledged ministers, continued the office he now holds and which he said was a sinecure. It seems to me that this vote involves a principle which should not be adopted by the committee. In a questiou of this kind one of two things should be done. Either the minister should come before parliament and explain exactly what the department needs in the shape of these buildings, and give the committee which is committing parliament and the country to the expenditure of money, the estimate of the total expenditure involved, or, if these plans are not forthcoming, if the minister is not able to give the committee this information, he should withhold the vote until he has that information to give us. By the plan now proposed, we are simply committing parliament to a policy of putting up these buildings at a cost which nobody now can estimate. Take this item as an example. By this vote we are committing parliament to the construction of this armoury. Suppose the minister comes next year and asks for a vote of $25,000 and tells us that if the money is not granted he will not be able to go on with the work and that the $10,000 already voted have been spent in acquiring a site or, in acquiring a site and putting up part of the building and will be of no avail.
Therefore the House will be obliged as it were to vote the $25,000 which the minister is asking for. It seems to me the system is wrong, the policy is wrong, it is almost unconstitutional to commit parliament to the expenditure of this money without parliament being perfectly aware of what is going to be done with it, and what policy the government is going to carry out. I cannot understand how it is unless the reason I gave this afternoon is a reason in this instance. Probably the constituency in which some of these buildings are to be erected are close constituencies. The town ot



Stratford in which this building is to be erected I believe is in a close constituency, and the vote is being held out as a bribe to the electors. They are told in the next election : If you do not vote for the government candidate the next time we sit in the House we will not give you enough to go on with the work. What hon. gentlemen condemned so much in the party which sits on this side of the House now, they are doing themselves, and doing to an extent greater than the Conservative party did it when they were in power. They are again going back upon the pledges and the oft repeated declarations which they made in opposition, and this is simply another instance of their inconsistency.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) I may tell him at once that I do not think I require a post office in Acton Vale to enable me to secure the support of the electors of that place. It is not for that consideration that I have endeavoured to obtain a post office for Acton Yale. I do not think, really, if I should be a candidate in the future, that the majority in Acton Vale could be more than it was in the election of 1900, because I had supporting me then most of the electors in that town. Regarding the population of Acton Vale I may say that it has been growing very much since the last census, due to the manufacturing; industries that we have built up since that time. At the present time if we had accommodation sufficient for the families of the employees that we have working for the company whose operations were commenced there last year we would need about thirty more houses. I hope that in a short time buildings will be put up and that these families will be living in Acton Vale. The building for which this appropriation is asked is not to _ be used only for the purposes of a post office. We are now talking of establishing another industry in the town and I hope that within a few days we will be in a position in connection with a new cigar factory to have a branch of the Inland Revenue Department organized there. I have asked the hon. Minister of Public Works to provide space in the new building for the Inland Revenue Department.
We have also in Acton Vale a militia com-panv of sixty-five members, and I have asked the minister to provide accommodation for the accoutrements of these volunteers. My hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) well knows that the county of Bagot has made very few claims on the public treasury, and the people of that county have in the past, as they will in the future, contributed their share to the construction of public works in other

parts of Canada. If my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) should do us the honour of visiting Acton Vale in the near future, perhaps when the general election comes, he will have an opportunity of seeing for himself that the town is not so unimportant as he seems to think it is.
Mr. CASGRAIN!. The hon. gentleman (Mr. J. E. Marcil) has presented no argument for the building of a post office in Acton Vale. He seems to express some doubt that he will be a candidate at the next election. Are we to suppose that he will be raised to a higher sphere ?

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I may be dead.

maintopic: SUPPLY - GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-INCOMPLETE CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I hope not. I rather supposed that the hon. gentleman expected to be elevated to that reward which has been the good luck of so many supporters of the Liberal party who have disappeared from this arena and gone to offices of ease and emolument. The hon. gentleman says the population of Acton Vale is growing, but he is not able to contradict the statement that the present population is 1,175. The reason he gives for the erection of a public building in Acton Vale is that he expects a factory will be established and that about thirty new houses will be required to accommodate the working people. Well, there would be just as much sense in the hon. gentleman asking the Minister of Public Works to build these thirty houses as there is in asking him to put up a public building in this small town. The hon. gentleman also expects a cigar factory in Acton Vale, but surely he is not treating the matter seriously when he makes such a plea as that for a public building. Where are we going to stop anyway, if we are going to erect public buildings in towns of 1,200 population ? If there is so much money lying around, I have no objection to public buildings being erected in the province of Quebec, but even so, there are many places in the province, the importance of which renders them more worthy the consideration of the government than the small town of Acton Vale.

That province has not received the justice to which it is entitled considering the revenue which is derived from it, as compared with the revenue received from some other provinces. In the city of Winnipeg, where I reside, the postal receipts for the months of September and October, 1902, from the sales of stamps were $12,000 and $15,000, respectively. For the months of September and October, 1903, the sales had increased from $12,000 and $15.000. respectively, to $18,000 and $21,000, respectively. Certainly there is no place in Canada, except Montreal and Toronto, where the postal revenue exceeds these amounts, and the sales of postage stamps in Winnipeg come well up to those of Toronto. So I say that the city of Winnipeg deserves any vote for extending its postal facilities which may he given.
